name: Florida

notes: Food for home consumption is exempt, but candy and soft drinks are taxed at the full rate, which is not counted here.
Household supplies: baby and toddler items (cribs, strollers, bottles, baby wipes, children's diapers) and adult incontinence products are exempt (since July 1, 2023), which is not taken out here.

Personal care products: menstrual products, oral hygiene products (toothbrushes, toothpaste, floss, mouthwash) and over-the-counter remedies are exempt, which is not taken out here; soap, shampoo and cosmetics are taxed.
Barber and beauty services, and laundry and dry cleaning: not taxed (FTA 2017 survey answer).

Clothing and shoes for children 5 and under are exempt (since July 1, 2023), and clothing and shoes of $100 or less are exempt during the annual back-to-school holiday (July 20 to August 20 in 2026); neither is taken out here.

Motor fuel is exempt from sales tax and taxed by the gallon instead: 32.025 cents in state taxes in 2026 (22-cent fuel tax, 9.9-cent SCETS, 0.125-cent inspection fee) plus 6 to 12 cents of county taxes, left out here; the rates are indexed each January 1, and the 2026 tax package had no gas tax holiday (reported).
Auto repair labor: taxed (FTA 2017 survey answer).
Counties add a discretionary sales surtax (local rates table).

Hurricane and safety items (smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, generators, tarps, batteries, sunscreen, insect repellent and others) have been exempt since August 1, 2025, which is not taken out of the home and personal care categories here (TIP 25A01-05).

Alcohol carries only per-gallon excise taxes paid by distributors besides the sales tax; Miami-Dade County adds food and beverage taxes, and Miami Beach, Bal Harbour and Surfside a resort tax (local rates table).

Stays of six months or less pay the 6% sales tax and county surtax plus county tourist development taxes (6% in Miami-Dade, Broward, Orange, Hillsborough, Duval, Pinellas and Palm Beach) and some city taxes (Miami Beach 7%, Bal Harbour and Surfside 4%), which are not counted here (DOR form DR-15TDT, October 2026).
Tobacco is assumed taxed at the general rate (excise taxes left out); not verified state by state.
gaps: Florida cities levy no sales tax of their own; every place takes its county surtax. Only Miami Beach, Bal Harbour and Surfside are listed as places with their own rate, for their 2% resort tax on restaurant food and drink, which is counted in their restaurant rate. Miami-Dade County's own food and beverage taxes are not counted (see the county's note). Panama City charges merchants a 1% fee on retail sales, often passed on to buyers, and Panama City Beach a business tax receipt of 1% of retail sales; neither is counted (see each city's note).
The surtax applies only to the first $5,000 of a single item's price; this matters little for the categories here.

Surtaxes that were to expire December 31, 2026, each noted on its county's page: Brevard (1%), Charlotte (1%), Liberty (0.5%) and Santa Rosa (0.5%) were renewed or replaced by voters on November 3, 2026 (unofficial counts), so those counties' rates continue.

1254700: Panama City charges merchants a 1% fee on retail sales (restaurants, stores, groceries and hotels among them), which many pass on to buyers as a separate line; the city says the fee is not a tax, so it isn't counted here (City of Panama City, Merchant License and 1% Fee).
1254725: Panama City Beach charges businesses a business tax receipt of 1% of retail sales; it is not a sales tax and isn't counted here, and the city's page doesn't say whether it may be passed on to buyers (City of Panama City Beach, Doing Business).
12009: Brevard County's sales surtax is 1% in 2026, but both its 0.5% surtaxes (1% in all) expire on December 31, 2026 (Florida Department of Revenue, Form DR-15DSS for 2026); voters renewed both on November 3, 2026, the Save Our Indian River Lagoon half-cent (199,684 for, 64,514 against) and the school facilities half-cent (181,665 for, 81,128 against), so the 1% continues (Brevard County Supervisor of Elections, unofficial count of November 4).
12015: Charlotte County's sales surtax is 1% in 2026, but its 1% surtax expires on December 31, 2026 (Florida Department of Revenue, Form DR-15DSS for 2026); voters approved its extension on November 3, 2026, 56,284 for and 38,396 against (Charlotte County Supervisor of Elections, unofficial count), so the 1% continues.
12041: Gilchrist County voters approved a countywide one cent (1%) sales surtax for emergency fire rescue services and facilities (the county commission's question, Gilchrist County Supervisor of Elections' sample ballot), from January 1, 2027 (Ordinance 2026-04, as reported by the Citrus County Chronicle), on November 3, 2026, 4,760 for and 2,854 against (Gilchrist County Supervisor of Elections, unofficial count). A surtax can start only on a January 1 (s. 212.054(5), F.S.); it is counted once the Department of Revenue's 2027 form lists it.
12077: Liberty County's sales surtax is 1.5% in 2026, but its 0.5% surtax expires on December 31, 2026 (Florida Department of Revenue, Form DR-15DSS for 2026); voters approved a new half-cent surtax for county-wide fire prevention and suppression services (Ordinance 2026-02) on November 3, 2026, 1,458 for and 1,121 against (Liberty County Supervisor of Elections, unofficial count), from January 1, 2027 through December 31, 2031, so the 1.5% continues; the expiring 0.5% is the county's emergency fire rescue surtax (Office of Economic and Demographic Research) and the new one is counted once the Department of Revenue's 2027 form lists it.
12086: Miami-Dade County levies two food and beverage taxes (s. 212.0306, F.S.): 2% on food and drink sold in hotels and motels, and 1% on food and drink, alcohol included, at other places licensed to serve alcohol on the premises with more than $400,000 a year in sales (veterans' organizations exempt; package sales aren't taxed). Both apply countywide except in Miami Beach, Bal Harbour and Surfside, which levy their own 2% resort tax on restaurant food and drink instead (Miami-Dade FY 2026-27 proposed budget). Neither county tax is in the restaurant figures here: each covers only some restaurants, which the spending categories don't separate.
12113: Santa Rosa County's sales surtax is 1% in 2026, but its 0.5% surtax expires on December 31, 2026 (Florida Department of Revenue, Form DR-15DSS for 2026); voters approved both half-cent questions on November 3, 2026, the county half-cent surtax (52,894 for, 19,484 against) and the school half-cent continuation (48,692 for, 23,509 against), so the expiring 0.5% continues (Santa Rosa County Supervisor of Elections, unofficial count).

programs: Community redevelopment areas are shown where a city or county publishes a map of them (Florida has no statewide map), so some aren't shown. The Rural Areas of Opportunity map (FloridaCommerce, March 2022) predates three additions: northeast Okaloosa and northern Bay County joined the Northwest area by Executive Order 25-141 (July 2025), and Nassau County joined the North Central area by Executive Order 26-56, amending Executive Order 23-132 (FDOT's list of rural designations, March 2026); each is noted on its county's page. The South Central area (DeSoto, Glades, Hardee, Hendry, Highlands and Okeechobee counties, Belle Glade, Pahokee, South Bay and Immokalee) was re-designated unchanged for five years by Executive Order 26-153 (July 21, 2026). South Walton is left out, since only the part of Walton County north of Choctawhatchee Bay is in the program.

Northeast Okaloosa County (east of State Road 85 and north of Interstate 10, with Laurel Hill and the unincorporated areas of Auburn, Deerland and Svea) joined the Northwest Rural Area of Opportunity by Executive Order 25-141 (July 2025; Okaloosa County release, July 11, 2025). It isn't on the program map shown here, which predates it.

Northern Bay County (north of Scotts Ferry Road and east of US 231, and north of State Road 388 between US 231 and State Road 79) joined the Northwest Rural Area of Opportunity by Executive Order 25-141 (July 2025), through July 2030 as reported (The Capitolist, July 8, 2025). It isn't on the program map shown here, which predates it.

Nassau County joined the North Central Rural Area of Opportunity by Executive Order 26-56, amending Executive Order 23-132 (FDOT's list of rural designations, March 2026); it isn't on the program map shown here, which predates it.

warn: Hurricane Idalia's storm surge flooded Horseshoe Beach in August 2023, and a year later Hurricane Helene's, estimated at more than 15 feet above ground, destroyed about 70% of the community (National Weather Service, Tallahassee: county impact reports of September 21, 2023 and October 14, 2024). Figures that include Horseshoe Beach come from before the storms and describe it as it was, not as it is now.

Hurricane Idalia's storm surge flooded Steinhatchee in August 2023, and a year later Hurricane Helene's, 12 to 16 feet above ground, devastated it: the National Hurricane Center reports that Helene destroyed about 80% of the buildings in Keaton Beach and Steinhatchee, and FEMA inspectors found 312 Steinhatchee homes that could not be lived in until repaired, 31 of them destroyed, after 132 such homes the year before (National Hurricane Center: Helene report, February 17, 2026; FEMA individual assistance registrations). Figures that include Steinhatchee come from before the storms and describe it as it was, not as it is now.

warn.text: Orlando draws many visitors (the theme parks and the convention center nearby, most of them outside the city limits), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: {visitor_why}. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Kissimmee draws many visitors (the hotels along U.S. 192 near the Walt Disney World resorts, many of them outside the city limits), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: {visitor_why}. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.
